heading: San Francisco
text:
- Population: 873,965 (2020 Census).
- Location: the Bay Area's anchor city, at the northern tip of the San Francisco Peninsula, on a peninsula bordered by the Pacific Ocean to the west and San Francisco Bay to the east. All "north/south/east/west of SF" references in this note set are measured from here.
- Highlight: dense, hilly, and historically the region's financial, cultural, and tourism center, home to the Golden Gate Bridge and a compact 7x7-mile street grid.

heading: Daly City
text:
- Population: 104,901 (2020 Census).
- Location: immediately south of San Francisco, the first city encountered driving south along the Peninsula on Highway 1 or I-280.
- Highlight: known for its foggy hillside neighborhoods and as a major gateway suburb connecting SF to the rest of the Peninsula.

heading: South San Francisco
text:
- Population: 66,105 (2020 Census).
- Location: south of San Francisco and just south of Daly City, at the northern end of the Peninsula's biotech corridor.
- Highlight: nicknamed "The Industrial City," it is now a hub for biotechnology companies, with a giant hillside sign reading "South San Francisco The Industrial City."

heading: San Mateo
text:
- Population: 105,661 (2020 Census).
- Location: on the Peninsula, south of San Francisco and south of South San Francisco, roughly halfway between SF and Palo Alto.
- Highlight: a central Peninsula suburb with a walkable downtown and the San Mateo Bridge connecting east to the East Bay.

heading: Redwood City
text:
- Population: 84,292 (2020 Census).
- Location: on the Peninsula, south of San Mateo and north of Palo Alto.
- Highlight: home to a major Oracle campus (Oracle's corporate headquarters relocated to Austin, Texas in December 2020).

heading: Menlo Park
text:
- Population: 33,780 (2020 Census).
- Location: on the Peninsula, south of Redwood City and just north of Palo Alto, bordering East Palo Alto.
- Highlight: headquarters of Meta (Facebook) and adjacent to Stanford University's land holdings.

heading: Palo Alto
text:
- Population: 68,572 (2020 Census).
- Location: on the Peninsula, south of Menlo Park, directly across San Francisco Bay from the East Bay city of Fremont.
- Highlight: home to Stanford University and considered a birthplace of Silicon Valley's startup culture.

heading: Mountain View
text:
- Population: 82,376 (2020 Census).
- Location: south of Palo Alto, on the southwest edge of the Bay, between the Peninsula and the South Bay.
- Highlight: headquarters of Google (Alphabet), with a downtown Castro Street known for tech-worker foot traffic.

heading: Sunnyvale
text:
- Population: 155,805 (2020 Census).
- Location: south of Mountain View, between Mountain View and Santa Clara.
- Highlight: a major Silicon Valley tech employment center, historically home to defense and semiconductor firms before today's software companies.

heading: Cupertino
text:
- Population: 60,381 (2020 Census).
- Location: southwest of Sunnyvale, in the western South Bay near the base of the Santa Cruz Mountains.
- Highlight: headquarters of Apple, including the ring-shaped Apple Park campus.

heading: Santa Clara
text:
- Population: 127,647 (2020 Census).
- Location: directly north of San Jose, between Sunnyvale and San Jose.
- Highlight: home to Levi's Stadium (the San Francisco 49ers' home field) and Santa Clara University.

heading: San Jose
text:
- Population: 1,013,240 (2020 Census).
- Location: at the southern end of San Francisco Bay, well south of SF and generally considered the South Bay's largest city and the unofficial "capital" of Silicon Valley.
- Highlight: the most populous city in the Bay Area and the third-most populous in California, though historically overshadowed in name recognition by San Francisco.

heading: Milpitas
text:
- Population: 80,273 (2020 Census).
- Location: northeast of San Jose, at the northern tip of the South Bay along the eastern shore.
- Highlight: a smaller tech-manufacturing hub with one of the Bay Area's largest shopping malls, the Great Mall.

heading: Oakland
text:
- Population: 440,646 (2020 Census).
- Location: directly across San Francisco Bay from SF (east of SF), reachable via the Bay Bridge; immediately south of Berkeley.
- Highlight: the East Bay's largest city, with a working port, a diverse population, and its own distinct downtown and arts scene separate from SF.

heading: Berkeley
text:
- Population: 124,321 (2020 Census).
- Location: on the east shore of the Bay, north of Oakland and directly across the Bay from SF and the Golden Gate.
- Highlight: home to the University of California, Berkeley, and a long history as a center of activism and academic research.

heading: Alameda
text:
- Population: 78,280 (2020 Census).
- Location: an island city just south of Oakland, connected by bridges and a tunnel, across the estuary from Oakland's downtown.
- Highlight: a former naval air station site, now known for its preserved Victorian-era housing stock and a small-town feel close to Oakland.

heading: Richmond
text:
- Population: 116,448 (2020 Census).
- Location: on the east shore of the Bay, north of Berkeley, connected to Marin County by the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge.
- Highlight: an industrial port city with a major oil refinery and growing waterfront redevelopment.

heading: Fremont
text:
- Population: 230,504 (2020 Census).
- Location: at the southeastern edge of the Bay, south of Oakland/Hayward, directly across the Bay from Palo Alto and Menlo Park.
- Highlight: home to Tesla's primary vehicle assembly plant and a large, diverse South Asian immigrant community.

heading: Hayward
text:
- Population: 162,954 (2020 Census).
- Location: on the east shore of the Bay, between Oakland/San Leandro to the north and Fremont to the south, connected to the Peninsula by the San Mateo Bridge.
- Highlight: a historically industrial and agricultural city, now a mid-Bay residential hub with California State University, East Bay.

heading: Walnut Creek
text:
- Population: 70,127 (2020 Census).
- Location: inland East Bay, northeast of Oakland and Berkeley, over the hills from the Bay shoreline.
- Highlight: a suburban retail and dining hub for the inland East Bay ("Contra Costa County"), less foggy than the Bay-facing cities.

heading: Concord
text:
- Population: 125,410 (2020 Census).
- Location: inland East Bay, north of Walnut Creek, further from SF than most Bay-shore cities.
- Highlight: the largest city in Contra Costa County, a commuter suburb with a large central park and amphitheater.

heading: Pleasanton
text:
- Population: 79,871 (2020 Census).
- Location: inland East Bay, southeast of Oakland and Hayward, near the junction of I-580 and I-680.
- Highlight: a corporate office hub (e.g., Workday) with a preserved historic downtown Main Street.

heading: Livermore
text:
- Population: 87,955 (2020 Census).
- Location: the easternmost major Bay Area city, east of Pleasanton, at the edge of the Bay Area before the Central Valley.
- Highlight: home to Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and a growing wine-country region (the Livermore Valley).

heading: San Rafael
text:
- Population: 61,271 (2020 Census).
- Location: in Marin County, north of San Francisco across the Golden Gate Bridge, the largest city in Marin.
- Highlight: Marin County's government and commercial center, at the base of hills leading to Mount Tamalpais.

heading: Vallejo
text:
- Population: 126,090 (2020 Census).
- Location: at the northern tip of San Francisco Bay, where it meets the Carquinez Strait, northeast of Richmond across the water.
- Highlight: a historic naval shipyard town (Mare Island Naval Shipyard, decommissioned 1996), now a more affordable North Bay commuter city.

heading: Napa
text:
- Population: 79,246 (2020 Census).
- Location: north of Vallejo, at the southern end of the Napa Valley wine region.
- Highlight: the commercial hub of Napa Valley, world-famous for wine tourism.

heading: Santa Rosa
text:
- Population: 178,127 (2020 Census).
- Location: in Sonoma County, northwest of Napa and the largest city in the North Bay.
- Highlight: the North Bay's commercial and government center, at the heart of Sonoma County's wine and agricultural region.

heading: Bay Area Sub-Regions Overview
text:
A short reference note defining the Bay Area's main sub-regions and how cities are typically grouped into them. Useful for orienting any city or neighborhood relative to the region as a whole.

## The five main sub-regions

- **San Francisco / The Peninsula**: San Francisco sits at the northern tip of a peninsula bounded by the Pacific Ocean (west) and San Francisco Bay (east). "The Peninsula" usually refers to the string of cities south of SF along that strip, from Daly City down through Palo Alto, before reaching the South Bay.
- **South Bay / Silicon Valley**: the cities ringing the southern end of San Francisco Bay, roughly from Mountain View and Sunnyvale through San Jose. This is the Bay Area's largest sub-region by population and the historic center of the tech industry.
- **East Bay**: the cities on the eastern shore of the Bay, reached from SF via the Bay Bridge. Divided informally into the Bay-facing cities (Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, Richmond) and the inland Contra Costa County cities further east (Walnut Creek, Concord, Pleasanton, Livermore).
- **North Bay**: Marin, Sonoma, and Napa Counties, north of San Francisco across the Golden Gate Bridge or north of Richmond across the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge. Includes San Rafael, Novato, Vallejo, Napa, Santa Rosa, and Petaluma.
- **Peninsula-to-South Bay corridor**: sometimes Redwood City, Menlo Park, Palo Alto, Mountain View, and Sunnyvale are grouped together as the corridor connecting the Peninsula to Silicon Valley proper, since the Bay narrows and the two areas blend together there.

## Orientation reference points

- Directions "north/south of San Francisco" in this wiki are measured along the Peninsula and North Bay axis, with San Francisco itself as zero point.
- Directions "north/south of Berkeley" refer to the East Bay's Bay-facing shoreline, where Richmond sits north of Berkeley and Oakland sits south of Berkeley.
- The Bay is crossed by several bridges: the Golden Gate Bridge (SF to Marin/North Bay), the Bay Bridge (SF to Oakland/East Bay), the San Mateo Bridge (Peninsula to Hayward/East Bay), the Dumbarton Bridge (Peninsula to Fremont/East Bay), and the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge (East Bay to Marin/North Bay).
- San Francisco Bay narrows to nothing at its southern end near San Jose, which is why the South Bay cities (San Jose, Santa Clara, Fremont) are considered to "close the loop" between the Peninsula and the East Bay.

## How this note connects to the wiki

This note is a geography reference for the two other source documents in this wiki: the Bay Area city profiles (`vault/raw/bay-area-cities.md`) and the San Francisco neighborhood profiles (`vault/raw/sf-neighborhoods.md`). Each city profile places a city within one of the sub-regions defined here; each SF neighborhood profile places a neighborhood relative to San Francisco as a whole, using the same city as the North Bay/East Bay reference point described above.

heading: Financial District
text:
- Location: northeast SF, the compact high-rise core just south of the Embarcadero waterfront.
- Highlight: the region's traditional banking and corporate headquarters district, and the densest cluster of skyscrapers in the city.

heading: North Beach
text:
- Location: north-central SF, just north of the Financial District and east of Russian Hill.
- Highlight: the city's historic Italian-American neighborhood, known for cafes, and adjacent to Chinatown.

heading: Chinatown
text:
- Location: north-central SF, just north of Union Square and west of the Financial District.
- Highlight: one of the oldest and most established Chinatowns in North America, dense with shops and residences.

heading: Nob Hill
text:
- Location: north-central SF, on a hilltop just west of the Financial District and northeast of Union Square.
- Highlight: historically home to the city's wealthiest 19th-century residents, known for grand hotels and cable car lines.

heading: Russian Hill
text:
- Location: north SF, west of North Beach and north of Nob Hill, close to the northern waterfront.
- Highlight: known for its steep, winding streets, including the famous switchback block of Lombard Street.

heading: Telegraph Hill
text:
- Location: northeast SF, east of North Beach, overlooking the northern waterfront and Bay.
- Highlight: topped by Coit Tower, with views over the Financial District and the Bay Bridge.

heading: Union Square
text:
- Location: central-north SF, just south of the Financial District's western edge.
- Highlight: the city's main shopping and theater district, centered on a public plaza.

heading: Tenderloin
text:
- Location: central SF, just west of Union Square and southeast of Nob Hill.
- Highlight: a dense, historically low-income neighborhood in the geographic middle of downtown, with significant social services.

heading: Hayes Valley
text:
- Location: central SF, west of Civic Center and north of the Mission District.
- Highlight: a boutique shopping and dining strip that emerged after a freeway removal opened up the area in the 1990s.

heading: Civic Center
text:
- Location: central SF, south of the Tenderloin, around SF's City Hall.
- Highlight: the city and county government center, including City Hall, main library, and performing arts venues.

heading: SoMa (South of Market)
group: South of Market and Eastern SF
text:
- Location: central-east SF, immediately south of Market Street and the Financial District.
- Highlight: a former industrial area now home to tech company offices, convention space (Moscone Center), and museums.

heading: Mission Bay
group: South of Market and Eastern SF
text:
- Location: southeast SF, south of SoMa along the eastern waterfront.
- Highlight: a newer, purpose-built district anchored by UCSF's biomedical campus and the Chase Center arena.

heading: Potrero Hill
group: South of Market and Eastern SF
text:
- Location: southeast SF, south of Mission Bay, on a hill east of the Mission District.
- Highlight: a sunnier hillside neighborhood with sweeping Bay views, historically industrial at its base.

heading: Dogpatch
group: South of Market and Eastern SF
text:
- Location: southeast SF, along the waterfront south of Mission Bay and east of Potrero Hill.
- Highlight: a former shipbuilding and industrial area now known for converted warehouse spaces and galleries.

heading: The Mission (Mission District)
text:
- Location: south-central SF, south of the Tenderloin/Hayes Valley area and east of the Castro.
- Highlight: a historically Latino neighborhood known for murals, taquerias, and one of the city's sunniest microclimates.

heading: The Castro
text:
- Location: south-central SF, west of the Mission District and south of Hayes Valley/Duboce Triangle.
- Highlight: internationally known as the center of San Francisco's LGBTQ+ community and history.

heading: Noe Valley
text:
- Location: south-central SF, directly south of the Castro.
- Highlight: a quieter, family-oriented neighborhood with a village-like main shopping street (24th Street).

heading: Twin Peaks
text:
- Location: geographic center of SF, west of Noe Valley and the Castro.
- Highlight: two hilltop summits offering the most panoramic views of the entire city and Bay.

heading: Excelsior
text:
- Location: south-central SF, south of the Mission District, bordered by John McLaren Park to the east.
- Highlight: a diverse, largely residential working-class neighborhood in the city's southern flatlands, centered along Mission Street.

heading: Pacific Heights
text:
- Location: north SF, west of Russian Hill and north of Japantown, on a ridge overlooking the Bay.
- Highlight: one of the city's wealthiest neighborhoods, known for grand mansions and Bay views.

heading: The Marina
text:
- Location: north SF, along the northern waterfront, west of Russian Hill and the Presidio's eastern edge.
- Highlight: a flat, waterfront neighborhood with views of the Golden Gate Bridge, popular for jogging and yacht harbors.

heading: The Presidio
text:
- Location: northwest corner of SF, at the foot of the Golden Gate Bridge.
- Highlight: a former U.S. Army post, now a national park with forests, trails, and coastal bluffs.

heading: Richmond District (Inner & Outer)
text:
- Location: northwest SF, north of Golden Gate Park, stretching from the park to the Pacific Ocean.
- Highlight: a foggy, residential district with a large Asian-American population and Clement Street's shopping corridor.

heading: Sunset District (Inner & Outer)
text:
- Location: southwest SF, south of Golden Gate Park, stretching from the park to the Pacific Ocean.
- Highlight: the city's largest residential district, known for foggy weather, rows of similar houses, and Ocean Beach.

heading: Golden Gate Park
text:
- Location: west-central SF, spanning the width of the city between the Richmond and Sunset districts.
- Highlight: a large landscaped park (bigger than New York's Central Park) with museums, gardens, and open lawns, forming the boundary between the northwest and southwest neighborhoods.
